results.title: Every level of a Claude second brain explained
results.summary: A second brain should start at the simplest level that solves your pain, progressing from a simple CLAUDE.md router to semantic search and knowledge graphs only if needed.

facts.label: Core Principle
facts.value: Find the lowest level that solves your pain

facts.label: Tool Agnostic
facts.value: System works with Claude Code, Cursor, Hermes Agent

sections.heading: Level 1: CLAUDE.md Router
items: Start with a CLAUDE.md file as a system prompt and router.
Basic folder structure: context (about me, stack), projects, decision log.
Goal: Stop re-explaining things; AI knows where to look for exact word/name matches.
Problem: Can get messy if it grows too big.

sections.heading: Level 2: Adding Wikis & Auto Memory
items: Builds on Level 1 by adding routing to wikis (e.g., LLM Wiki, YouTube transcript wiki).
Wikis organize files by topic (e.g., agentic workflows, AI coding) with backlinks.
Claude Code can auto-update a memory.md file.
Presenter's own Herk2 project sits primarily at this level.

sections.heading: Level 3: Semantic Search (Vector Databases)
items: Introduces semantic search via tools like Pinecone or Supabase.
Searches based on meaning, not keyword matching.
Good for retrieving specific answers from large text datasets (e.g., finding rule 17 out of 1000).
Not ideal for tasks requiring full context (e.g., summarizing a meeting transcript).
Can be mixed with markdown files; not everything needs to be vectorized.

sections.heading: Level 4: Knowledge & Relationship Graphs
items: Most complex and potentially expensive level.
Maps relationships between entities (e.g., clients, projects).
Requires significant data input; can use a 'Grill Me' skill to interview and generate data.
Presenter does not use this day-to-day as his project-based work doesn't require it.

sections.heading: Level 5: Full Autonomy
items: Always-on autonomous system.
Not necessarily the best goal; Level 5 isn't for everyone.

steps: Start with Level 1 (CLAUDE.md router and basic folders).
Identify a specific pain point in your current system.
Move to a higher level only if it solves that pain (e.g., add a wiki for topic aggregation, use semantic search for specific retrieval).
Mix and match levels for different data types within the same second brain.
tips: Design your data structure backwards: start with how you'll query the data in the future.
Your system doesn't need to be visually complex (like Obsidian graphs) to be effective.
Be mindful of privacy: sending data to cloud models like Claude means it's not private.
Use the 'Grill Me' skill to rapidly generate data for knowledge graphs.

Lead with your vision, not your background or roadmap.
Engineer takeaways by presenting compelling points, not raw data.

results.title: Key patterns for scaling Claude Code in large codebases
results.summary: The most successful deployments treat AI context as architecture, using a layered CLAUDE.md approach where root files hold global rules and subdirectory files define local exceptions, with regular pruning to avoid stale context.

facts.label: Primary success factor
facts.value: Treating context as architecture, not documentation

facts.label: Key failure mode
facts.value: Stale context loading into every session

sections.heading: Effective CLAUDE.md Structure
items: Root-level file for non-negotiable global conventions
Subdirectory-level files for local exceptions and team-specific rules
Context nearest the working directory is given higher weight by the model
This creates inheritance without conflicts, similar to CSS cascading

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls
items: One giant rulebook does not scale
Stacking too many rules in a single file causes the model to skip important ones
Old local rules can quietly steer major changes if not pruned
Code can be current while AI follows yesterday's stale rules

sections.heading: Critical Success Factors
items: Pre-existing strong engineering practices and disciplined teams
Creating the right development workflow, not just the model
Quality of instructions matters more than model size
Automating context review or having a human DRI responsible for it

quotes.text: The interesting question you're skipping is whether 'most successful deployments' just means teams that already had strong engineering practices and would have succeeded with almost any decent tool.
Scaling AI tools across large codebases is less about the model itself and more about creating the right development workflow.

The CLAUDE.md layering approach is underrated. Having context load automatically as you navigate the directory tree means the model always has the right conventions in scope without you having to think about it.

results.title: Best ever chocolate brownies recipe
results.summary: This classic recipe yields fudgy brownies with a shiny crust by melting dark chocolate with butter, folding it into whipped eggs and sugar, and baking for 25-35 minutes.

items: 185g unsalted butter
185g best dark chocolate
85g plain flour
40g cocoa powder
50g white chocolate
50g milk chocolate
3 large eggs
275g golden caster sugar

steps: Cut butter into cubes and break dark chocolate into pieces. Melt together in a bowl over a pan of hot water or in a microwave for 2 minutes on High. Let cool to room temperature.
Preheat oven to 180C/160C fan/gas 4. Line a 20cm square tin with foil or parchment.
Sift plain flour and cocoa powder together into a bowl.
Chop white chocolate and milk chocolate into chunks.
In a large bowl, whisk eggs and golden caster sugar with an electric mixer on maximum speed for 3-8 minutes until very pale, thick, and creamy, and the mixture leaves a trail.
Pour the cooled chocolate mixture over the egg mixture and gently fold together with a figure-of-eight motion until combined.
Sift the flour and cocoa mixture over the chocolate-egg mixture and gently fold in until the mixture looks fudgy.
Stir in the chopped white and milk chocolate chunks.
Pour the mixture into the prepared tin, spread into corners, and level the top.
Bake for 25 minutes. Check by gently shaking the tin; if the middle wobbles, bake for another 5 minutes until the top has a shiny crust and sides pull away.
Leave in the tin until completely cold, then lift out and cut into 16 squares or 32 triangles.
tips: Store in an airtight container for up to two weeks or freeze for up to a month.
